source.title: Back to Normal Symmetry? Biomechanical Variables Remain More Asymmetrical Than Normal During Jump and Change-of-Direction Testing 9 Months After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction

paper.citation: King, E., Richter, C., Franklyn-Miller, A., Wadey, R., Moran, R., & Strike, S. (2019). Back to normal symmetry? Biomechanical variables remain more asymmetrical than normal during jump and change-of-direction testing 9 months after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. The American Journal of Sports Medicine, 47(5), 1175–1185. https://doi.org/10.1177/0363546519830656
paper.abstract: Are performance and biomechanical asymmetries during jump and change-of-direction tasks greater in male athletes nine months after primary ACL reconstruction than in matched healthy multidirectional field-sport athletes? The ACL-reconstruction group included 156 male multidirectional field-sport athletes aged 18–35 who intended to return to the same level; 62 healthy male field-sport athletes formed the matched comparison cohort. Testing occurred 8–10 months after primary reconstruction following locally supervised progressive rehabilitation. Previous ACL surgery, multiple ligament reconstruction, meniscal repair, full-thickness chondral injury, and lack of return intent were exclusion criteria. Case-control laboratory study using double- and single-leg drop jumps, single-leg hop for distance, and planned and unplanned 90° cuts. Eight-camera motion capture synchronized with force platforms quantified three-dimensional kinematics and kinetics; three valid trials per limb were averaged. Root-mean-square limb difference quantified asymmetry without choosing a denominator, and statistical parametric mapping compared waveform asymmetry between groups.
paper.tldr: This controlled laboratory study shows why acceptable task outcomes can coexist with altered movement strategies during late-stage ACL rehabilitation. Across tasks, nearly all significant group differences indicated greater biomechanical asymmetry after ACL reconstruction, especially in sagittal- and frontal-plane variables. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Case-control laboratory study using double- and single-leg drop jumps, single-leg hop for distance, and planned and unplanned 90° cuts. Eight-camera motion capture synchronized with force platforms quantified three-dimensional kinematics and kinetics; three valid trials per limb were averaged. Root-mean-square limb difference quantified asymmetry without choosing a denominator, and statistical parametric mapping compared waveform asymmetry between groups.
paper.findings: Across tasks, nearly all significant group differences indicated greater biomechanical asymmetry after ACL reconstruction, especially in sagittal- and frontal-plane variables. Jump tasks exposed more between-group asymmetry than change-of-direction tasks; sagittal-plane differences appeared consistently across jump tests. Single-leg hop distance asymmetry did not differ between groups despite multiple biomechanical asymmetry differences, showing that performance symmetry can mask strategy differences. Change-of-direction time differences were small even when force and joint variables differed, so time alone did not fully represent rehabilitation status.
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional comparison cannot determine whether asymmetry caused reinjury, reflected incomplete rehabilitation, or was an adaptive strategy. Root-mean-square difference captures magnitude but not which limb or strategy produced the asymmetry. Findings may not generalize to female athletes, adolescents, or non-field-sport populations. The clinical importance of some statistically identified differences is unknown; change-of-direction time asymmetry differed by only 0.03 seconds. The study did not establish prospective return-to-play or reinjury thresholds.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not clear or classify an athlete from hop distance or cut time alone. Pair task outcomes with force-time and movement-strategy information when available, and compare both limbs with healthy task expectations and the athlete's own history. Use asymmetry as one dimension of a broader rehabilitation decision, not a universal cutoff.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Do not clear or classify an athlete from hop distance or cut time alone. Pair task outcomes with force-time and movement-strategy information when available, and compare both limbs with healthy task expectations and the athlete's own history. Use asymmetry as one dimension of a broader rehabilitation decision, not a universal cutoff. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, do not clear or classify an athlete from hop distance or cut time alone. Pair task outcomes with force-time and movement-strategy information when available, and compare both limbs with healthy task expectations and the athlete's own history. Use asymmetry as one dimension of a broader rehabilitation decision, not a universal cutoff. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
